screens.title: Understanding the Core Requirements and Scope
screens.narratorSegment: When you design a social media feed, the most important step is not drawing boxes but asking precise questions. In this chapter you will learn how to separate functional needs — the concrete behaviors users expect — from non-functional constraints like scalability, availability, and latency. We'll show you how to list core entities such as User, Post, Follow, Like, and Comment, and how to turn primary user flows into measurable requirements. For example, instead of saying “the system should scale,” you will learn to ask for peak queries per second and acceptable feed latency targets. That matters because those numbers determine caches, databases, and replication strategies. You will also practice spotting premature technical solutions and common mistakes, like choosing a messaging system before estimating throughput. By the end of this lesson, you will be able to produce a clear scope statement for a feed system and identify which requirements must be strongly consistent versus those that tolerate eventual consistency. Think about a recent social app you used: what would you measure first to size its feed?

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Understanding the Core Requirements
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson: define, measure, and scope a social feed.

Understand Core Requirements and Scope

We will distinguish functional behaviors from non-functional constraints, identify core entities and user flows, and surface the measurable numbers that drive design decisions for a social feed system.

Core Entities Map
User
Post
Follow
Interaction
These core objects will define your data model and primary flows.
Why scope matters

Scope translates vague goals like “scale well” into measurable targets. Those targets guide storage, cache, and queue choices early on.

Explore Key Topics
Functional Req.
User, Post, Follow, Like, Feed generation.
Non-Functional
Scalability, availability, latency, durability.
Scope & Metrics
QPS/TPS targets, peak vs concurrent users.
Coming up: a method to capture requirements, translate them into numbers, and prioritize features for an MVP feed that meets real user expectations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these lessons you'll be able to identify and categorize the functional requirements of a social feed system, and to define the non-functional constraints that determine architecture. You will practice converting vague needs into measurable targets like feed read QPS and acceptable latency ranges. You will learn to list the core entities — User, Post, Follow, Like, Comment — and to map the primary user flows such as creating a post, following a user, and viewing a personalized feed. Finally, you will learn to spot premature technical proposals and instead prioritize requirements by risk and cost. For example, when asked about scaling a feed, you'll know to request expected peak writes per second and the percentage of reads that must be served within a specific latency. These skills matter because they let you size caches, databases, and message systems appropriately and avoid needless over-engineering. Consider an app that suddenly needs to support ephemeral stories; your ability to re-evaluate priorities and estimate new QPS helps make pragmatic design choices.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Verification
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on how you will demonstrate mastery. You will learn to capture metrics for peak and concurrent usage, to estimate QPS and TPS for reads and writes, and to produce a short prioritization document for feature rollout. A useful exercise is to take an example requirement such as short-video uploads and estimate peak upload TPS, resulting storage needs, and CDN bandwidth. You will also practice forming clarifying questions: how many daily active users, what percent are concurrent, and what is acceptable feed staleness. These clarifying questions reduce ambiguity and stop teams from choosing systems that don't match real load. Finally, you will record at least one trade-off: where to accept eventual consistency for the sake of speed and where to demand strong consistency. The verification milestone will be a short checklist: a scoped entity model, a list of measurable targets, and a prioritized roadmap that maps requirements to risk and cost. These artifacts are what interviewers and product owners want to see, and they make design choices defensible.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Learning Objectives
Practice Tasks
  1. Estimate peak post writes and feed read QPS for an MVP audience.
  2. Map entities and mark which fields must be strongly consistent.
  3. Produce a prioritized features list with estimated cost drivers.
  4. Create one clarifying question set to reduce ambiguity in requirements gathering.
Mnemonic: Ask, Measure, Map, Prioritize.
Verification Checklist
  • Entity diagram with primary relationships and cardinality.
  • Numeric targets: expected peak QPS/TPS, acceptable latency.
  • Priority classification for features: Critical, High, Medium, Low.
  • One paragraph justification for trade-offs chosen.
Follow this checklist to make requirements defensible and design decisions traceable.

screens.title: Functional Requirements for a Social Feed
screens.narratorSegment: Functional requirements describe the concrete behaviors your feed system must provide. Start by writing short user stories: a user can register and authenticate, create content, follow another user, like or comment, and view a personalized feed. Each of these stories implies specific data and operations. For example, user registration implies a secure profile store, hashed credentials, and session tokens. Posting content implies persisted media, metadata fields like timestamp and author, and possibly moderation steps. Following creates directed edges in the social graph and becomes the core input to feed generation. When you capture functional requirements, be precise about the observable behavior: what fields a Post has, whether likes increment immediately, and whether deleted posts vanish from followers' feeds. A concrete example: "When Alice posts a photo, Bob — who follows Alice — should see that photo in his feed within a few seconds." A common misconception is to treat functional and non-functional requirements interchangeably; they are different questions. Functional requirements are not satisfied by scaling alone — they define the flows you must build and test. Your immediate takeaway is to document each user flow with preconditions, data produced, and success criteria. Which user flow would you test first to prove basic feed functionality?

keyIdea.title: Write precise user stories
keyIdea.text: Translate high-level features into concrete user flows and data artifacts to avoid ambiguity.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Functional Requirements
Definition & Examples

Functional requirements specify the behaviors users expect. They become the primary acceptance tests for your feed system.

  • User Registration: create account, secure credentials, session tokens.
  • Posting Content: text, image, video storage and metadata like timestamp and author.
  • Following: directed social graph to determine who sees which posts.
  • Liking/Commenting: interactions that update counts and show on feeds.
  • Feed Generation: produce a personalized ordered stream for each user.
Concrete Example
When Alice posts, Bob must see the post in his feed within defined staleness limits. Preconditions: Bob follows Alice and has an active session.
Testable Acceptance Criteria
  1. Given a new post from a user, followers should see it within X seconds.
  2. Given a like action, the displayed count should update within Y seconds.
  3. Given account creation, the user can authenticate and access their feed securely.
Key Takeaway

Capture functional needs as user stories with preconditions and measurable success criteria before choosing infrastructure.

screens.title: From Post to Feed: The Data Flow
screens.narratorSegment: A post travels through several stages from creation to appearing in followers' feeds. First, the user submits content which the A P I persists: a Post object with metadata. Next, any media is stored in durable storage and referenced by the post. Then the social graph is consulted to determine recipients: followers or followers-of-followers depending on the model. Finally, the feed generation step either pushes the post to recipients' timelines or records it for on-demand aggregation on read. These two patterns — push and pull — are critical trade-offs. In a push model, writes fan out to many timelines at write time, increasing the write cost but making reads fast. In a pull model, reads aggregate from multiple sources, making writes cheap but reads expensive and potentially slower. Concrete example: if Alice has a million followers, pushing at write time may blow up write costs; pulling may be chosen, but you'll need aggressive caching. A common misconception is assuming one approach is universally better; the right choice depends on QPS, follower distribution, and read/write ratios. Consider a high-read, low-write ratio: pushing to timelines for active users can improve latency. Which trade-offs does your expected workload suggest?

keyIdea.title: Push vs Pull trade-off
keyIdea.text: The feed data flow choice between push and pull drives the cost and latency characteristics of your system.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › From Post to Feed
Process Steps
1.
Client submits post → API validates and persists Post object.
2.
Media saved to durable object store; Post stores media reference.
3.
Social graph lookup finds followers or delivery targets.
4.
Feed delivery: push to timelines or record for on-demand aggregation.
Comparison: Push vs Pull
Push (Fan-out)
Writes expensive; reads cheap and fast. Good for heavy-read, low-write scenarios.
Pull (Fan-in)
Writes cheap; reads aggregate at query time. Better when followers are many or writes are frequent.
Concrete Scenario
If a celebrity posts, pushing to millions of timelines is costly. A pull model with caching may be more cost-effective for that edge case.

screens.title: Non-functional Requirements: The Decision Drivers
screens.narratorSegment: Non-functional requirements determine the engineering strategy and component choices. Scalability asks how the system behaves as users and posts increase, and whether we scale horizontally for reads, writes, or both. Availability sets uptime expectations and guides redundancy and failover design. Latency places a cap on how long a feed retrieval can take before users feel the app is slow. Durability ensures published posts are not lost. Consistency defines where strong correctness is mandatory and where eventual consistency is acceptable. Cost-effectiveness ties all these together — high availability and low latency at massive scale are expensive, so trade-offs are inevitable. A concrete contrast: demanding sub-100 millisecond feed reads globally will push you toward aggressive edge caching and replicated read stores, increasing cost. A common misconception is to default to strong consistency everywhere; doing so can dramatically limit scalability and increase latency. In practice, choose strong consistency for authentication and user profile updates but allow eventual consistency for like counts and feed ordering when it improves throughput. Your job is to map each requirement to components and acceptable error modes so that design decisions are guided by business priorities.

keyIdea.title: Trade-offs are explicit
keyIdea.text: Non-functional targets convert product goals into architecture constraints that require explicit trade-offs between cost and performance.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Non-functional Requirements
Definitions & Implications
  • Scalability: ability to add resources to handle more work. Drives sharding and replication choices.
  • Availability: uptime requirements that guide redundancy, failover, and SLA targets.
  • Latency: acceptable response times; affects caching and edge strategies.
  • Durability: guarantees that data persists even after failures; backup and replication policies follow.
  • Consistency: where immediate correctness is required and where eventual consistency is acceptable.
  • Cost-effectiveness: balancing infrastructure cost against performance and availability goals.
Decision Grid
Strong Consistency
Use for auth, billing, profile updates where correctness is essential.
Eventual Consistency
Acceptable for like counts or feed propagation where slight delays are tolerable.
Practical Example
If you require 99.99% uptime and <200ms feed loads, expect a significant cost premium for global replication and edge caching. Decide which markets need full guarantees.

screens.title: Core Entities and Data Model
screens.narratorSegment: Defining core entities and their relationships is a foundational task. At minimum, model User, Post, Follow, Like, and Comment. For each entity, list required fields, indexes, and access patterns. For example, a Post should include id, author id, timestamp, media references, and aggregated counts. Indexes on author id and timestamp support a user's posts timeline. The Follow entity represents a directed edge and may require efficient reads for follower lists and writes for follow/unfollow operations. Consider cardinality: some users will have few followers while others (celebrities) may have millions; that distribution impacts storage and delivery choices. Likes and Comments are interaction entities that drive counters and notification events; counters can be maintained eventually consistent to reduce contention. A common pitfall is denormalizing too early without measuring read/write ratios; while denormalization can speed reads, it raises complexity for updates and deletes. A concrete approach is to sketch the entity with required fields and add two columns: typical QPS for reads and writes. This mapping surfaces hotspots and helps decide whether to shard, cache, or offload heavy operations to background jobs. What field or index would you add first to speed feed generation for active users?

keyIdea.text: Design entities with fields and indexes driven by read/write patterns and follower cardinality distributions.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Core Entities
Entity Cards
User
id, username, hashed credentials, profile metadata, privacy flags. Index by id and username.
Post
id, author_id, timestamp, media_refs, text, like_count, comment_count. Index by author and time.
Follow
follower_id, followee_id, created_at. Optimize reads for followee's followers and follower's followees.
Like / Comment
interaction records and counters. Counters may be eventually consistent to avoid hotspots.
Design Decisions
  • Estimate per-entity QPS/TPS to identify bottlenecks.
  • Plan sharding by author id or geographic region where necessary.
  • Use denormalized timelines for heavy-read users and on-demand aggregation for sparse users.
Common Mistake
Designing a single table for all posts without considering hot rows for popular authors, which causes write contention and uneven load.

screens.title: Acceptance Criteria and Measurable Targets
screens.narratorSegment: A strong design starts with measurable acceptance criteria. Instead of saying the feed should be "fast," specify acceptable latency, target QPS/TPS, and staleness windows. For example, require that 95 percent of feed reads return in under 200 milliseconds, and that post propagation occurs within 5 seconds for typical followers. Translate business expectations into numbers: how many daily active users, what percent are concurrent, and what is the expected read-to-write ratio. A common mistake is estimating "millions of users" without specifying peak or concurrent rates; those numbers determine sharding and cache sizing. A practical way to capture these targets is a short table or template where each requirement is paired with priority and estimated peak QPS/TPS. Below is a template you can use in an interview to show you can reason about scale. Always accompany your numbers with justification: for instance, assume 10 million DAU with 10% concurrent equals one million concurrent users, and multiply by average reads per user to produce feed read QPS. This practice shows interviewers you can convert product language into engineering inputs. Acceptance Criteria and Measurable Targets means concrete targets for latency, qps, and staleness are necessary inputs for sizing and selecting components.. In practical terms, turn vague statements into numeric requirements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Acceptance Criteria
Requirement Template
Requirement: Feed read latency
Priority: Critical
Target: 95% of feed reads < 200ms
Estimated Peak QPS: 200,000 reads/sec
Justification: Assume 10M DAU, 20% active concurrently, averaging 10 feed reads/minute per active user.
Use this format to justify component choices in interviews and design docs.
How to estimate
  1. Start with DAU, pick a concurrency percentage.
  2. Multiply by average feed interactions per minute to get reads/sec.
  3. Apply peak multipliers for spikes and buffer for growth.
Check Your Understanding
Given 5M DAU and 15% concurrency with 5 reads/minute per active user, what is approximate read QPS? Try the template to compute and justify your answer.

screens.title: Notifications and Real-time Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Notifications are a special case of the feed problem that impose near-real-time constraints. Requirements might include delivering likes, mentions, or comments within seconds. To meet this, systems often use pub/sub or message queues to propagate events to notification services and to mobile push gateways. The choice of protocol and persistence affects durability and retry behavior. For instance, a fire-and-forget push reduces latency but risks message loss unless backed by durable queues. A common misconception is to treat notifications and feed retrieval the same; they have different patterns and SLAs. Notifications are often small payloads and require immediate delivery, whereas feed reads can tolerate slight staleness and larger payloads. A concrete scenario: when Alice comments on Bob's post, Bob should see a notification in under three seconds. Achieving that at scale implies scalable fan-out systems and careful handling of bursts — such as batching or rate-limiting notification sends. Your architecture choices here will affect availability and cost, so link notification SLAs explicitly to product needs before choosing technology. Notifications and Real-time Considerations means real-time delivery requirements for notifications often require separate event systems, durable queues, and burst-handling strategies.. In practical terms, how immediacy requirements influence architecture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Real-time delivery requirements for notifications often require separate event systems, durable queues, and burst-handling strategies.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Notifications
What notifications require
  • Low delivery latency (seconds).
  • Durable event persistence and retry mechanisms.
  • Scalable fan-out or batching for bursts.
  • Separation of notification SLAs from feed SLAs.
Concrete Flow
1.
User action generates event → persisted to durable queue.
2.
Notification service consumes events, formats payload, and dispatches to push gateway or in-app stream.
3.
Backpressure handling: batch, throttle, or store for retry on downstream failures.
Common Mistake
Tightly coupling notification delivery to main write path which increases end-to-end latency and failure blast radius. Use async pipelines instead.

screens.title: Scope Definition: User Flows and Bottlenecks
screens.narratorSegment: Establishing scope requires mapping primary user flows and identifying where bottlenecks are likely to appear. Key flows include: user logs in, creates a post, follows another user, views a feed, and interacts with posts. For each flow, annotate expected read and write operations, data touched, and whether the operation is latency-sensitive. For example, viewing a feed touches reads across many friends' posts, sorting or ranking logic, and possibly cached timelines. Creating a post is a write-heavy operation that needs durability and quick acknowledgment but can defer expensive downstream propagation. Recognize hotspots like celebrity writes, which create fan-out storms, or read-heavy feeds that stress caches. Use a simple timeline or matrix to record peak QPS/TPS per flow and mark operations that need strong consistency. A common misconception is to treat all flows equally in priority; in reality a small number of flows often consume most resources. Your immediate action is to produce a flow map and label the likely scaling levers: caching, sharding, background workers, or CDN. Which flow would you prioritize for caching in an early MVP? Module 11 › Chapter 11.1 › Scope & Flows
Primary User Flows
  1. Login: auth checks and profile read (strong consistency).
  2. Create post: write to Post store, media upload, queue propagation.
  3. Follow/unfollow: update social graph, possibly update timelines.
  4. View feed: aggregate or read precomputed timeline, apply ranking.
  5. Interact (like/comment): write interaction and update counters/notifications.
Hotspot Matrix
Write-heavy: Post creation, media storage.
Read-heavy: Feed retrieval, search.
Latency-sensitive: Feed reads, notifications.
Example Decision
Prioritize caching for feed reads in markets with most active users, and use background fan-out for less-active users.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Early Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent early mistake is to propose specific technologies before you have measured requirements. Saying “we'll use Kafka” or “we'll shard by user ID” without estimated throughput or distribution data can lead to expensive rework. Another common error is underestimating concurrency and peak loads: planning for average load often leaves systems brittle under spikes. Also avoid treating data consistency uniformly — some data needs strong correctness while others tolerate eventual updates. For example, likes and counters can often be eventually consistent, whereas authentication must be correct immediately. Cost is another trap: designing for five-nines availability across all subsystems dramatically increases cost. A concrete example: if you assume only tens of thousands of reads per second, and the actual peak is hundreds of thousands, caching and read-replica design chosen early may be insufficient. The right approach is iterative: gather target metrics, design a baseline to meet them, and reserve high-cost patterns for the critical parts. Always record assumptions explicitly — they become the criteria for future refactoring or scaling decisions. What assumption could you list first for your feed MVP? screens.title: Safety, Security, and Privacy Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Security and privacy are not afterthoughts; they shape data models and storage decisions. From the earliest requirements capture, specify protections against common web threats and compliance needs. For example, include XSS and CSRF protections in acceptance criteria for content rendering, require hashed credentials and secure session handling for authentication, and define retention and deletion policies for compliance with data privacy rules. Data minimization strategies — storing only what you need and purging when required — influence schema design. Durability requirements should account for encrypted backups and safe deletion mechanisms. A common misconception is to defer privacy considerations until later; once data is stored incorrectly, retrofitting compliance can be expensive and risky. A concrete checklist item: for each entity, specify whether data requires encryption at rest, whether it is subject to deletion requests, and how long metadata must be retained. Include these items in the scope doc so that design choices — like which fields to replicate to analytics clusters — respect privacy constraints. What privacy requirement would change your data replication plan? Safety, Security, and Privacy Considerations means specify threat mitigation, encryption, and retention rules as part of entity definitions and acceptance criteria.. In practical terms, build protection into requirements and models from day one. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. If users can request deletion, your system must propagate deletes to caches and replicas or keep soft-deletes until fully purged, which affects storage and operations.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Summarize the essential ideas you should remember. First, separate functional requirements from non-functional constraints: functional requirements define behavior, while non-functional constraints determine how well those behaviors must perform. Third, model your core entities and user flows early: User, Post, Follow, Like, Comment — annotate fields, indexes, and access patterns to expose hotspots. These concepts are why interviews focus on measurement and trade-offs, not just component names. Keep these three ideas in mind as you scope any feed system: write down explicit assumptions, pick the simplest design to meet measured targets, and plan to iterate. fullNarratorScript:
When you design a social media feed, the most important step is not drawing boxes but asking precise questions. In this chapter you will learn how to separate functional needs — the concrete behaviors users expect — from non-functional constraints like scalability, availability, and latency. We'll show you how to list core entities such as User, Post, Follow, Like, and Comment, and how to turn primary user flows into measurable requirements. For example, instead of saying “the system should scale,” you will learn to ask for peak queries per second and acceptable feed latency targets. That matters because those numbers determine caches, databases, and replication strategies. You will also practice spotting premature technical solutions and common mistakes, like choosing a messaging system before estimating throughput. By the end of this lesson, you will be able to produce a clear scope statement for a feed system and identify which requirements must be strongly consistent versus those that tolerate eventual consistency. Think about a recent social app you used: what would you measure first to size its feed?

By the end of these lessons you'll be able to identify and categorize the functional requirements of a social feed system, and to define the non-functional constraints that determine architecture. You will practice converting vague needs into measurable targets like feed read QPS and acceptable latency ranges. You will learn to list the core entities — User, Post, Follow, Like, Comment — and to map the primary user flows such as creating a post, following a user, and viewing a personalized feed. Finally, you will learn to spot premature technical proposals and instead prioritize requirements by risk and cost. For example, when asked about scaling a feed, you'll know to request expected peak writes per second and the percentage of reads that must be served within a specific latency. These skills matter because they let you size caches, databases, and message systems appropriately and avoid needless over-engineering. Consider an app that suddenly needs to support ephemeral stories; your ability to re-evaluate priorities and estimate new QPS helps make pragmatic design choices.

This second objectives screen focuses on how you will demonstrate mastery. You will learn to capture metrics for peak and concurrent usage, to estimate QPS and TPS for reads and writes, and to produce a short prioritization document for feature rollout. A useful exercise is to take an example requirement such as short-video uploads and estimate peak upload TPS, resulting storage needs, and CDN bandwidth. You will also practice forming clarifying questions: how many daily active users, what percent are concurrent, and what is acceptable feed staleness. These clarifying questions reduce ambiguity and stop teams from choosing systems that don't match real load. Finally, you will record at least one trade-off: where to accept eventual consistency for the sake of speed and where to demand strong consistency. The verification milestone will be a short checklist: a scoped entity model, a list of measurable targets, and a prioritized roadmap that maps requirements to risk and cost. These artifacts are what interviewers and product owners want to see, and they make design choices defensible.

Functional requirements describe the concrete behaviors your feed system must provide. Start by writing short user stories: a user can register and authenticate, create content, follow another user, like or comment, and view a personalized feed. Each of these stories implies specific data and operations. For example, user registration implies a secure profile store, hashed credentials, and session tokens. Posting content implies persisted media, metadata fields like timestamp and author, and possibly moderation steps. Following creates directed edges in the social graph and becomes the core input to feed generation. When you capture functional requirements, be precise about the observable behavior: what fields a Post has, whether likes increment immediately, and whether deleted posts vanish from followers' feeds. A concrete example: "When Alice posts a photo, Bob — who follows Alice — should see that photo in his feed within a few seconds." A common misconception is to treat functional and non-functional requirements interchangeably; they are different questions. Functional requirements are not satisfied by scaling alone — they define the flows you must build and test. Your immediate takeaway is to document each user flow with preconditions, data produced, and success criteria. Which user flow would you test first to prove basic feed functionality?

A post travels through several stages from creation to appearing in followers' feeds. First, the user submits content which the A P I persists: a Post object with metadata. Next, any media is stored in durable storage and referenced by the post. Then the social graph is consulted to determine recipients: followers or followers-of-followers depending on the model. Finally, the feed generation step either pushes the post to recipients' timelines or records it for on-demand aggregation on read. These two patterns — push and pull — are critical trade-offs. In a push model, writes fan out to many timelines at write time, increasing the write cost but making reads fast. In a pull model, reads aggregate from multiple sources, making writes cheap but reads expensive and potentially slower. Concrete example: if Alice has a million followers, pushing at write time may blow up write costs; pulling may be chosen, but you'll need aggressive caching. A common misconception is assuming one approach is universally better; the right choice depends on QPS, follower distribution, and read/write ratios. Consider a high-read, low-write ratio: pushing to timelines for active users can improve latency. Which trade-offs does your expected workload suggest?

Non-functional requirements determine the engineering strategy and component choices. Scalability asks how the system behaves as users and posts increase, and whether we scale horizontally for reads, writes, or both. Availability sets uptime expectations and guides redundancy and failover design. Latency places a cap on how long a feed retrieval can take before users feel the app is slow. Durability ensures published posts are not lost. Consistency defines where strong correctness is mandatory and where eventual consistency is acceptable. Cost-effectiveness ties all these together — high availability and low latency at massive scale are expensive, so trade-offs are inevitable. A concrete contrast: demanding sub-100 millisecond feed reads globally will push you toward aggressive edge caching and replicated read stores, increasing cost. A common misconception is to default to strong consistency everywhere; doing so can dramatically limit scalability and increase latency. In practice, choose strong consistency for authentication and user profile updates but allow eventual consistency for like counts and feed ordering when it improves throughput. Your job is to map each requirement to components and acceptable error modes so that design decisions are guided by business priorities.

Defining core entities and their relationships is a foundational task. At minimum, model User, Post, Follow, Like, and Comment. For each entity, list required fields, indexes, and access patterns. For example, a Post should include id, author id, timestamp, media references, and aggregated counts. Indexes on author id and timestamp support a user's posts timeline. The Follow entity represents a directed edge and may require efficient reads for follower lists and writes for follow/unfollow operations. Consider cardinality: some users will have few followers while others (celebrities) may have millions; that distribution impacts storage and delivery choices. Likes and Comments are interaction entities that drive counters and notification events; counters can be maintained eventually consistent to reduce contention. A common pitfall is denormalizing too early without measuring read/write ratios; while denormalization can speed reads, it raises complexity for updates and deletes. A concrete approach is to sketch the entity with required fields and add two columns: typical QPS for reads and writes. This mapping surfaces hotspots and helps decide whether to shard, cache, or offload heavy operations to background jobs. What field or index would you add first to speed feed generation for active users?

A strong design starts with measurable acceptance criteria. Instead of saying the feed should be "fast," specify acceptable latency, target QPS/TPS, and staleness windows. For example, require that 95 percent of feed reads return in under 200 milliseconds, and that post propagation occurs within 5 seconds for typical followers. Translate business expectations into numbers: how many daily active users, what percent are concurrent, and what is the expected read-to-write ratio. A common mistake is estimating "millions of users" without specifying peak or concurrent rates; those numbers determine sharding and cache sizing. A practical way to capture these targets is a short table or template where each requirement is paired with priority and estimated peak QPS/TPS. Below is a template you can use in an interview to show you can reason about scale. Always accompany your numbers with justification: for instance, assume 10 million DAU with 10% concurrent equals one million concurrent users, and multiply by average reads per user to produce feed read QPS. This practice shows interviewers you can convert product language into engineering inputs. In practical terms, turn vague statements into numeric requirements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Notifications are a special case of the feed problem that impose near-real-time constraints. Requirements might include delivering likes, mentions, or comments within seconds. Summarize the essential ideas you should remember. First, separate functional requirements from non-functional constraints: functional requirements define behavior, while non-functional constraints determine how well those behaviors must perform. Second, convert vague goals into measurable targets — define expected QPS, acceptable latency, and durability needs — because those numbers are what drive architecture and cost. Third, model your core entities and user flows early: User, Post, Follow, Like, Comment — annotate fields, indexes, and access patterns to expose hotspots. These concepts are why interviews focus on measurement and trade-offs, not just component names.
